overview.title: AI's climb up the spectrum of generalization
overview.main_topic: Mapping the history of AI onto the spectrum of generalization (automatons, local, broad, extreme), defining broad generalization, and arguing that deep learning is cognitive automation rather than intelligence; opening of 19.3 How to build intelligence.
overview.central_idea: AI has moved from pure automatons to local generalization and may be approaching broad generalization, but deep learning remains cognitive automation. Its models map X to Y through a smooth transform learned from dense data, which breaks under disruption, while human cognition achieves extreme generalization.
overview.importance: This page closes section 19.2 with a verdict on deep learning: it is enormously useful cognitive automation but not intelligence. It then opens section 19.3, which asks what is needed to build real intelligence and sets up the rest of the chapter.
learning_objectives: Place ELIZA, SHRDLU, 1990s–2000s machine learning and 2010s deep learning on the spectrum of generalization.
Define broad generalization and distinguish it from local and extreme generalization.
Explain the author's distinction between 'cognitive automation' and 'artificial intelligence' within 'artificial cognition'.
State precisely why deep learning models are limited to local generalization.
Recognize the question that 19.3 sets out to answer.
prerequisites: p.599: the spectrum of generalization in biological evolution.
p.598: local generalization, known unknowns, dense sampling.
Chapter 5: generalization via interpolation on a latent manifold.

summary:
The 19.2.4 sentence ends: certain hominins reached extreme generalization, **'precipitating the start of the Anthropocene'** and changing the history of life on Earth.

**AI's history follows the same climb.** Early AI systems were **pure automatons**: ELIZA (1960s chatbot) and SHRDLU (a 1970 system that manipulated simple objects from natural-language commands; footnote 2: Winograd). The 1990s–2000s brought **machine learning with local generalization**, able to handle some uncertainty and novelty. The 2010s brought **deep learning**, which expanded local generalization by allowing much larger datasets and more expressive models.

**Next step: broad generalization**, defined as dealing with **unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks**, including situations the system wasn't trained for and its creators couldn't anticipate. Examples: a self-driving car that safely handles anything, or a domestic robot passing the **'Woz test'** of entering a random kitchen and making coffee (footnote 3). Combining deep learning with **painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world** is making visible progress.

**A category error.** Deep learning remains **cognitive automation**. Calling it 'intelligence' is a category error. The field would be better named **'artificial cognition'**, with **cognitive automation** and **artificial intelligence** as two nearly independent subfields. AI proper is a 'greenfield' where almost everything remains to be discovered.

**Credit where due.** Cognitive automation is very useful, and learning to automate tasks from data alone is more practical and versatile than explicit programming, a game changer for nearly every industry. But models still only **map space X to space Y via a smooth geometric transform learned from a dense sampling of X-to-Y data points**, and **any disruption** in X or Y invalidates the mapping. Humans achieve extreme generalization and long-term planning.

**19.3 How to build intelligence** opens: there is much more to intelligence than latent manifold interpolation, so what are the core missing pieces?

paragraphs.what_it_says: Completing p.599: hominins trending toward extreme generalization precipitated the start of the Anthropocene and forever changed the history of life on Earth.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The Anthropocene is the proposed name for the period in which human activity is the dominant influence on Earth's environment. The author's point is that the jump to extreme generalization was so powerful that one species came to reshape the planet.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It conveys the stakes of the capability the chapter is about. Extreme generalization is not a small upgrade over local generalization; in biology it was transformative.

terminology.meaning: A proposed geological epoch defined by humanity's significant impact on Earth's geology and ecosystems.

connections: p.599: the start of the sentence on the spectrum of generalization.

paragraphs.excerpt: The progress of AI over the past 70 years bears striking similarities to
paragraphs.what_it_says: AI's 70-year history resembles biological evolution. Early systems were pure automatons, like ELIZA (1960s) or SHRDLU (1970), which manipulated simple objects from natural-language commands. In the 1990s and 2000s came machine learning systems with local generalization that could handle some uncertainty and novelty. In the 2010s deep learning expanded that local generalization by letting engineers use much larger datasets and much more expressive models.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The author places AI eras on the spectrum from p.599. **ELIZA** used hand-written pattern-matching rules to rephrase user input as questions, and **SHRDLU** worked in a tiny 'blocks world' with hand-coded grammar and logic. Both are pure if-then automatons that failed outside their scripted scope. Statistical ML learned mappings from data and could interpolate (local generalization). Deep learning made that interpolation far more powerful because the model family is more expressive and can absorb far more data. It moved along the same rung of the ladder, not up to a new one.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This explains why deep learning's successes, however large, do not by themselves show progress toward intelligence in the author's sense. They show progress in local generalization. It also ties chapter 1's history of AI to this chapter's theory.

terminology.meaning: A 1960s chatbot (Joseph Weizenbaum, MIT) that simulated a psychotherapist using scripted pattern-matching rules.
Terry Winograd's natural-language system (c. 1970) that manipulated objects in a simulated blocks world from typed commands.

connections: p.599: biological intelligence's climb up the spectrum of generalization.
p.620: chapter 20 recap: AI, machine learning and deep learning as nested approaches, with machine learning taking off in the 1990s.

paragraphs.excerpt: Today, we may be on the cusp of the next evolutionary step.
paragraphs.what_it_says: We may be near the next step: systems with broad generalization, defined as dealing with unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks, including situations the system wasn't trained for and its creators couldn't anticipate. Examples: a self-driving car that safely handles any situation, or a domestic robot passing the 'Woz test of intelligence' by entering a random kitchen and making a cup of coffee. By combining deep learning with painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world, we're already making visible progress.
paragraphs.what_it_means: **Broad generalization** is the rung between local and extreme. Compared with local generalization, it handles **unknown** unknowns, not just anticipated, sampled variation (p.598's known unknowns). Compared with extreme generalization, it is limited to **one domain** (driving, kitchens) rather than arbitrary novel situations. The Woz test makes this concrete: every kitchen is different (layout, appliances, where the mugs are), so the robot cannot have seen it before, but the domain is bounded. The current recipe of deep learning plus **handcrafted** world models means humans supply the abstractions, not the system.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a realistic near-term target and names the current workaround: engineers compensate for deep learning's lack of abstraction by hand-building it (maps, physics models, rule-based safety layers). That is progress, but the abstraction is not learned, which is the gap the rest of the chapter addresses.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Formally the three levels differ in what they handle: local handles test inputs near the training distribution; broad handles distribution shifts, anticipated or not, within a domain; extreme handles new domains and tasks with little or no data.

terminology.meaning: The ability to deal with unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks, including situations neither the training data nor the creators anticipated.
Factors of variation or situations that were not anticipated and are not represented in the training data.
Steve Wozniak's proposed test: a robot enters an unfamiliar home and makes a cup of coffee (footnote 3: Fast Company, March 2010).

connections: p.598: known unknowns, the limit of local generalization.
p.597: extreme generalization, the top of the spectrum.

paragraphs.excerpt: However, the deep learning paradigm has remained limited to cognitive automation: The “intelligence”
paragraphs.what_it_says: The deep learning paradigm has stayed limited to cognitive automation, and the 'intelligence' label in 'artificial intelligence' has been a category error. A more accurate name for the field would be 'artificial cognition', with 'cognitive automation' and 'artificial intelligence' as two nearly independent subfields. Under this division, AI is a greenfield where almost everything remains to be discovered.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A **category error** is attributing a property to something of the wrong kind. The author argues that systems that automate cognitive tasks have been described as having intelligence, which they don't. The proposed taxonomy separates two goals: **cognitive automation** (getting machines to perform specific cognitive tasks such as recognizing images, translating, or answering exam questions) and **artificial intelligence** (machines that can adapt to novelty efficiently). They are 'nearly independent': progress on one tells you little about the other.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This reframing explains how a field can show spectacular, real progress (cognitive automation) while making little progress on its namesake goal (intelligence). It encourages readers to evaluate claims of 'AI progress' by asking which subfield the result belongs to.

terminology.meaning: Automating specific cognitive tasks (perception, translation, Q&A) without the ability to adapt to novelty; what deep learning does.
Ascribing to something a property that belongs to a different kind of thing.
The author's proposed umbrella name for the field, containing cognitive automation and artificial intelligence.
An undeveloped area where work starts from scratch.

connections: p.597: the field 'has long suffered from conflating the notions of intelligence and automation'.
p.603: task-specific successes 'without featuring any intelligence'.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now, I don’t mean to diminish the achievements of deep learning.
paragraphs.what_it_says: This is not meant to diminish deep learning. Cognitive automation is very useful, and deep learning's ability to automate tasks from exposure to data alone is a particularly powerful form of it, far more practical and versatile than explicit programming and a game changer for nearly every industry. But it is still far from human or animal intelligence. Our models only perform local generalization: they map space X to space Y via a smooth geometric transform learned from a dense sampling of X-to-Y data points, and any disruption within X or Y invalidates this mapping. They only generalize to situations similar to past data, while human cognition achieves extreme generalization, adapting quickly to radically novel situations and planning for long-term future situations.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This paragraph is the most precise technical statement of deep learning's limit in the section. Its parts: **'map space X to space Y'**: a model is a function $f_\theta: X \to Y$. **'Smooth geometric transform'**: $f_\theta$ is a composition of differentiable layers, a continuous deformation of the input space (the 'uncrumpling paper ball' view from early chapters). **'Learned from a dense sampling of X-to-Y data points'**: the parameters $\theta$ are fitted so $f_\theta$ matches training pairs, which needs good coverage. **'Any disruption ... invalidates this mapping'**: if the input distribution shifts (X changes) or the meaning of outputs changes (Y changes), the fitted surface no longer applies, and the model cannot re-derive it without new data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It balances the critique: deep learning is the most powerful cognitive automation tool available and is worth mastering (the purpose of this book). Being clear about its limit tells practitioners when to expect failure: distribution shift, new task definitions, long-horizon planning.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Smoothness is both the strength and the limit. A smooth $f_\theta$ makes interpolation between nearby training points reliable (local generalization), but smoothness says nothing about regions with no data, and nothing in a fixed $f_\theta$ can adapt when the X-to-Y relation itself changes.

terminology.meaning: Writing the rules of a task by hand, as opposed to learning them from data.
A continuous, differentiable mapping from input space to output space, as implemented by a deep network.

paragraphs.excerpt: So far, you’ve learned that there’s a lot more to intelligence than the
paragraphs.what_it_says: Opening 19.3: there is much more to intelligence than the latent manifold interpolation deep learning does. So what is needed to start building real intelligence, and what core pieces are currently missing?
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sets the agenda for the rest of the chapter. The answer comes in steps: the kaleidoscope hypothesis (why abstraction is possible, p.601), intelligence as abstraction acquisition plus on-the-fly recombination (p.602), setting the right target and measuring adaptation (pp.602–607), and the missing ingredients of search and symbols (section 19.4, p.608 onward).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It marks the transition from diagnosing the problem (19.1–19.2) to proposing solutions (19.3–19.4).

terminology.meaning: Generalizing by moving between known training points along a learned low-dimensional data manifold; deep learning's mechanism (chapter 5).

connections: p.608: 19.4 the missing ingredients: search and symbols.

paragraphs.excerpt: 2 Terry Winograd, “Procedures as a Representation for Data in a Computer Program
paragraphs.what_it_says: Footnote 2 cites Terry Winograd, 'Procedures as a Representation for Data in a Computer Program for Understanding Natural Language,' 1971, the source of SHRDLU. Footnote 3 cites Michael Shick, 'Wozniak: Could a Computer Make a Cup of Coffee?' Fast Company, March 2010, the source of the Woz test.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The SHRDLU work is Winograd's MIT doctoral thesis. The text calls SHRDLU 'a 1970 AI' while the cited report is dated 1971; the system was developed around 1968–1970 and the report published afterward, so the dates are consistent. In the 2010 interview, Wozniak suggested that a robot walking into an unfamiliar home and making coffee would be a meaningful test of machine intelligence.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: They let readers trace the two concrete examples to primary sources.

concepts.name: Broad generalization
concepts.definition: The ability to deal with unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks, including situations the system was not trained to handle and that its creators could not have anticipated.
concepts.intuition: A driver who has never seen this particular road, weather or detour but still drives safely: novelty is unbounded, but it is still driving.
concepts.technical: It sits between local generalization (known unknowns near the training data) and extreme generalization (radically novel situations across domains, with little or no data).
concepts.significance: The author names it as the next evolutionary step for AI, currently approached by combining deep learning with handcrafted abstract world models.
concepts.example: A fully robust self-driving car; a domestic robot passing the Woz coffee test.
concepts.misconception: That a self-driving car working well in the cities it was tested in shows broad generalization; it must handle situations no one anticipated.

concepts.name: Cognitive automation
concepts.definition: Automating specific cognitive tasks with systems that do not adapt to novelty; what the deep learning paradigm has achieved.
concepts.intuition: Machines that can do a cognitive job very well, rather than machines that can figure out new jobs.
concepts.technical: Deep learning implements it by learning a smooth geometric transform from X to Y from a dense sampling of examples, which the author calls far more practical and versatile than explicit programming.
concepts.significance: The author proposes 'artificial cognition' as the field's umbrella, split into cognitive automation and artificial intelligence, two nearly independent subfields.
concepts.example: Image classification, machine translation, answering exam questions from training data.
concepts.misconception: That cognitive automation is unimportant. The author calls it 'a game changer for essentially every industry'.

concepts.name: Spectrum of generalization (applied to AI)
concepts.definition: Ordering systems by how broadly they generalize: pure automatons, local, broad, extreme.
concepts.intuition: AI history as a ladder: scripted chatbots, then statistical ML, then deep learning (a better version of the same rung), then the hoped-for broad, then extreme.
concepts.technical: ELIZA and SHRDLU were pure automatons; 1990s–2000s ML and 2010s deep learning provide local generalization; broad generalization is the next step; extreme generalization remains human-level.
concepts.significance: It lets you judge AI progress by generalization power rather than task scores.
concepts.example: Deep learning's leap in the 2010s expanded local generalization but did not reach broad generalization.
concepts.misconception: That bigger models automatically move up a rung; the author argues deep learning scaled local generalization.

deeper.title: The three rungs side by side
deeper.body:
Summarizing pp.597–600 (book content, tabulated here):

| Level | Handles | Data needed | Examples on these pages |
|---|---|---|---|
| None | Only exactly pre-specified cases | n/a | Python dict, if-then-else Q&A, ELIZA, SHRDLU |
| Local | Known unknowns near training data | Dense sampling | 1990s–2000s ML, 2010s deep learning, insect brains |
| Broad | Unknown unknowns within one domain | ? (target) | Robust self-driving car, Woz-test robot |
| Extreme | Radically novel situations across domains | Little or none | Humans (and, to a degree, advanced animals) |

deeper.title: What 'any disruption within spaces X or Y' looks like in practice
deeper.body:
Illustrative examples (not from the book):

- **Disruption in X (input distribution shift):** a medical-imaging model trained on one hospital's scanners sees images from a different manufacturer; the pixel statistics move off the learned manifold and accuracy drops.
- **Disruption in Y (output/task change):** a sentiment model trained for 'positive/negative' is asked to detect sarcasm, or a product taxonomy changes. The meaning of outputs changes and the old mapping no longer applies.

In both cases the standard remedy is to collect new data and retrain or fine-tune. That is the dense-sampling route again, the opposite of the little-or-no-data adaptation of extreme generalization.

deeper.title: Why handcrafted world models are a telling workaround
deeper.body: The author says progress toward broad generalization currently comes from 'combining deep learning and painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world'. Inference: this hybrid shows where each part's strength lies. Deep learning provides perception (local generalization from data). The handcrafted parts (HD maps, traffic rules, physics-based motion planning) provide **abstractions that hold beyond the training data**, but humans write them. A system that could *acquire* such abstractions itself would be moving from cognitive automation toward intelligence, which is the program of 19.3–19.4.

misconceptions.claim: Deep learning moved AI from local to broad generalization.
misconceptions.correction: The author says deep learning 'further expanded the local generalization power' of ML systems; broad generalization is a next step we 'may be on the cusp of'.
He explicitly says he doesn't mean to diminish it. Cognitive automation from data is 'far more practical and versatile than explicit programming' and 'a game changer for essentially every industry'.

misconceptions.claim: Broad generalization means handling anything in any domain.
misconceptions.correction: It is restricted to unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks. Handling radically novel situations across domains is extreme generalization.

misconceptions.claim: 'Artificial intelligence' and 'cognitive automation' are two names for the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: The author proposes treating them as two nearly independent subfields of 'artificial cognition'. Progress in one does not imply progress in the other.

takeaways: Reaching extreme generalization let hominins start the Anthropocene.
AI's history mirrors evolution: pure automatons (ELIZA, SHRDLU), then ML with local generalization, then deep learning with expanded local generalization.
Broad generalization means handling unknown unknowns within a single broad domain; examples are a fully robust self-driving car and a robot passing the Woz coffee test.
Deep learning is cognitive automation; calling it 'intelligence' is a category error. The author proposes 'artificial cognition' split into cognitive automation and AI.
Deep models map X to Y via a smooth geometric transform learned from dense X-to-Y samples; any disruption in X or Y invalidates the mapping.
Section 19.3 asks what core pieces are missing to build real intelligence.

questions.question: Define broad generalization as the author does, and give one of his examples.
questions.answer: The ability to deal with unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks, including situations the system was not trained for and that its creators could not have anticipated. Examples: a self-driving car that safely handles any situation, or a domestic robot passing the Woz test (making coffee in a random kitchen).
questions.explanation: Defined in the paragraph beginning 'Today, we may be on the cusp...'.

questions.question: Where does the author place 2010s deep learning on the spectrum of generalization?
options: Local generalization, expanded by larger datasets and more expressive models
questions.answer: Local generalization, expanded by larger datasets and more expressive models
questions.explanation: The text: 'In the 2010s, deep learning further expanded the local generalization power of these systems.' ELIZA-style automatons are earlier, broad generalization is the next step we 'may be on the cusp of', and extreme generalization is human cognition.

questions.question: Why does the author call the 'intelligence' label in 'artificial intelligence' a category error, and what alternative naming does he propose?
questions.answer: Because the deep learning paradigm has remained limited to cognitive automation, so calling it intelligence attributes a property it does not have. He proposes calling the field 'artificial cognition', with 'cognitive automation' and 'artificial intelligence' as two nearly independent subfields, the latter a greenfield.
questions.explanation: From the paragraph beginning 'However, the deep learning paradigm...'.

questions.question: Explain each part of the sentence 'they map space X to space Y via a smooth geometric transform learned from a dense sampling of X-to-Y data points, and any disruption within spaces X or Y invalidates this mapping.'
questions.answer: A model is a function from inputs X to outputs Y. It is a smooth, differentiable geometric transformation, a composition of layers. It is fitted to many example pairs that must cover the input space densely. If the input distribution changes or the meaning of outputs changes, the fitted function no longer applies and can't adapt without new data.
questions.explanation: Each phrase corresponds to a concept from earlier chapters (layers as geometric transforms, dense sampling from chapter 5) and to local generalization (p.598).

questions.question: According to the page, how is visible progress toward broad generalization currently being made?
options: By scaling deep learning models alone
By combining deep learning with painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world
By returning to ELIZA-style rule systems
questions.answer: By combining deep learning with painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world
questions.explanation: Stated directly. Scaling alone is what section 19.2 ('Scale isn't all you need') argues against. Pure rule systems are automatons, and evolutionary algorithms are not mentioned here.

questions.question: What were ELIZA and SHRDLU, and why does the author call them pure automatons?
questions.answer: ELIZA was a 1960s chat program; SHRDLU was a 1970 system that manipulated simple objects from natural-language commands. They are pure automatons because they followed hand-written rules and could not generalize beyond what was explicitly programmed.
questions.explanation: The page names both as early pure automatons; footnote 2 cites Winograd's work behind SHRDLU.

questions.question: Classify a recent AI product you know as cognitive automation or (toward) artificial intelligence in the author's sense, and justify it using the X-to-Y mapping criterion.
questions.answer: Open answer. A good answer asks whether the system only maps inputs similar to its training data to outputs (cognitive automation) or whether it can adapt with little or no data to situations nobody anticipated.
questions.explanation: Practices applying the page's distinction to real claims of AI progress.
